name: Des Moines International Airport
before:
Iowa's main airport, five miles south west of Des Moines, and a joint civilian and military field. The 132nd Wing of the Iowa Air National Guard is based here, so military movements sit alongside the airlines.

Six carriers serve it: American, Allegiant, Delta, Frontier, Southwest and United. Traffic reached a record 2.92 million passengers in 2019.

The terminal has two concourses. Concourse A holds gates A1 to A5 and is used by Allegiant, Southwest and United. Concourse C holds gates C1 to C7 for American, Delta, Frontier and Allegiant. A renovation finished in 2010 made every gate common use, so an airline can be moved between them at short notice, which is worth knowing if a client is checking a gate number the night before.

The site covers around 2,600 acres with two runways, both a little over 9,000 feet, at an elevation of 958 feet.
after:
Iowa's main airport, five miles south west of Des Moines. It is a joint civilian and military field, and the 132nd Wing of the Iowa Air National Guard is based here.

American, Allegiant, Delta, Frontier, Southwest and United all fly from Des Moines. The FAA's preliminary figures show almost 1.6 million passengers boarding flights here in 2025.

Its site covers around 2,600 acres, with two runways of a little over 9,000 feet each, at an elevation of 958 feet.

claims.note: Wikipedia does not say it in words. Iowa DOT lists the state's eight commercial service airports, and the FAA's CY2025 table has all eight: Des Moines 1,596,784 boardings, Cedar Rapids (The Eastern Iowa) 801,353, then Sioux City, Waterloo, Fort Dodge, Mason City, Dubuque and Burlington, each under 30,000.

claims.claim: military movements sit alongside the airlines
claims.wasBefore: so military movements sit alongside the airlines
claims.why: An inference with no second source. Wikipedia itself says the 132nd Wing stopped flying F-16s in 2013 and now does intelligence, surveillance and cyber work, so its own flying from the airport is not established; the FAA record shows military ramps but no traffic figures. The joint civil and military use is kept.

The count rests on Wikipedia alone: the airport's own airline list (flydsm.com) is behind a CAPTCHA bot check and BTS counts operating carriers, regional partners included. The six airline names are kept, each with a current source.

claims.wasBefore: Traffic reached a record 2.92 million passengers in 2019.
claims.why: Out of date: the FAA's 2024 and 2025 boardings (1,555,454 and 1,596,784) are well above 2019's level, and Wikipedia's infobox gives 3,254,107 total passengers for 2025. Replaced by the FAA's 2025 figure, attributed.

claims.claim: two concourses, gates A1 to A5 and C1 to C7, and which airlines use them
claims.wasBefore: The terminal has two concourses. Concourse A holds gates A1 to A5 and is used by Allegiant, Southwest and United. Concourse C holds gates C1 to C7 for American, Delta, Frontier and Allegiant.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The airport's own site (flydsm.com), where the maps and gate lists are, answers with a CAPTCHA 'Human Verification' bot check, so it could not be used. A new terminal is being built (see the held-back entry), so the gate layout is likely to change: worth checking by hand.

claims.claim: a 2010 renovation made every gate common use
claims.wasBefore: A renovation finished in 2010 made every gate common use, so an airline can be moved between them at short notice, which is worth knowing if a client is checking a gate number the night before.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The architect's project page (BBS Architects Engineers) mentions a common-use passenger processing system but gives no date and does not say every gate is common use; the airport's own site is behind a CAPTCHA bot check.

Held back: a new terminal replaces nothing in the old text. For Andy: Wikipedia and the City of Des Moines both describe a new terminal (Wikipedia: $445 million, 18 gates at first, groundbreaking October 2023, 'scheduled to open in 2026'; the City: Phase 1A of 265,000 square feet with five new gates and 18 in all, 'first phase slated for completion in 2026' and later phases through 2027). Neither page is dated within the last 12 months, and the airport's own Lift DSM page, which would give the current date, is behind a CAPTCHA bot check, so the opening date needs checking by hand before it is added.

sources.quote: The airport broke ground on a new, larger terminal in October 2023. The $445 million project is the centerpiece of the LiftDSM initiative and will replace the current 1948-era terminal. The new facility will initially feature 18 gates, increasing the airport's capacity by 50%, and is scheduled to open in 2026.

quote: Phase 1A of the Des Moines International Airport expansion encompasses a 265,000-square-foot terminal featuring five new gates
Upon completion, the terminal will offer a total of 18 gates
Construction commenced in 2023, with the first phase slated for completion in 2026 and subsequent phases extending through 2027.
sources.dated: read 2026-09-23 (live page, no date of its own)
